mcqs.question: What makes a piece of added flexibility "over-engineering" rather than good design?
options: It uses more than one design pattern in the same file
It was written by a junior engineer instead of a senior one
It takes more than a day to implement
Its cost — more files, more indirection, more onboarding time — is paid immediately, for a benefit deferred to a speculative future that may never arrive
mcqs.explanation: The defining trait is the cost/benefit timing mismatch: the tax is paid now, unconditionally, while the payoff depends on a future need that might never materialize. Number of patterns used, author seniority, and implementation time aren't what makes something over-engineered — a quick, single-pattern addition can still be speculative and unnecessary.

mcqs.question: What's the practical test for whether an abstraction (a factory, a strategy interface) is premature?
options: Whether it has more than 50 lines of code
Whether you can point to two real, current call sites that need genuinely different behavior
Whether the class name ends in a suffix like "Factory" or "Strategy"
Whether it was reviewed and approved by a senior engineer
mcqs.explanation: The concrete test is real, current variation — if only one implementation exists and only one caller needs it, the abstraction has no second case to justify it yet. Line count, naming convention, and review approval don't determine whether an abstraction is actually needed; a well-reviewed, well-named class can still be solving a problem that doesn't exist.

mcqs.question: According to the comparison, what's the key difference between appropriate abstraction and speculative generality?
options: Appropriate abstraction is always simpler code, measured in fewer total lines
Speculative generality only occurs in statically typed languages
Appropriate abstraction always uses interfaces, while speculative generality always uses inheritance
Appropriate abstraction is driven by two or more real, current call sites needing different behavior; speculative generality is driven by an imagined future need
mcqs.explanation: The distinguishing factor is what's driving the abstraction — real, present variation versus an anticipated one. Appropriate abstraction isn't necessarily fewer lines (it often adds some structure), speculative generality isn't language-specific, and neither is defined by whether it uses interfaces versus inheritance.

mcqs.question: Why is "we might need this later" a weak justification for adding an abstraction now?
options: It's unfalsifiable — almost anything might be needed eventually — and a guess made now is often shaped wrong for the real requirement when it actually arrives
It's a valid justification as long as the abstraction is well-documented
It's only weak when the codebase is written in a dynamically typed language
It's weak because "later" always means more than one year away
mcqs.explanation: The problem is that the justification can't be tested or disproven, so it can rationalize nearly unlimited speculative structure, and abstractions guessed at ahead of the real need often don't fit it when it shows up. Documentation doesn't fix an unfounded justification, the argument isn't language-specific, and there's no fixed time threshold that makes "later" acceptable or not.

mcqs.question: What's a more constructive way to challenge a possibly over-engineered design in code review than saying "this is over-engineered"?
options: Approve it anyway to avoid an uncomfortable conversation with the author
Ask a specific question like "what's the second implementation this interface is designed for?" so the author can justify it on its merits
Rewrite the code yourself without discussing it with the author first
Escalate the concern directly to the author's manager before commenting on the pull request
mcqs.explanation: A specific, answerable question invites justification rather than putting the author on the defensive — if there's a real second case, you learn it; if not, they often reconsider on their own. Silently approving avoids the actual problem, rewriting unilaterally bypasses the author, and escalating past them skips the direct, lower-friction conversation that usually resolves it.

mcqs.question: Why might duplicating two similar-looking pieces of validation logic be preferable to immediately extracting a shared abstraction?
options: Duplication is always faster to write, which is the only consideration that matters

If the two pieces represent different concepts that only coincidentally look alike today, sharing an abstraction couples them, and undoing that coupling later is riskier than deleting a duplicated function would have been
Shared abstractions are never appropriate under any circumstances
Code duplication has no maintenance cost whatsoever, so it's always the safe default
mcqs.explanation: The real risk being weighed is reversibility: a wrong shared abstraction that call sites grow dependent on differently is expensive to unwind, while removing a duplicated function is a simple, local change — that asymmetry is why premature sharing can be worse than the duplication it avoided. This isn't a blanket claim that abstraction is never right or that duplication is free of cost — it's specifically about which mistake is cheaper to walk back.
